summary:
Hoa Lich is an interactive web application that explores how satellite-detected fire activity across Vietnam changes over time. Using NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS and VIIRS, we harmonize detection counts into a common Suomi-NPP-equivalent scale to help users compare historical activity across different satellite records.

Users can select a location or region, explore maps and calendars, and compare activity across days, months, and years. Historical charts reveal seasonal patterns, while data-source information explains whether values come from direct observations, cross-satellite scaling, or model estimates. A bilingual Vietnamese–English interface makes these insights accessible to local users and international audiences.

By turning satellite records into understandable visual comparisons, Hoa Lich supports the challenge of understanding where and when burning occurs. It helps users investigate changes while clearly communicating uncertainty: satellite detections indicate observed fire activity, rather than confirmed wildfire incidents or burned area.
details:
Hoa Lich is a bilingual web application that helps users explore the history of satellite-detected fire activity in Vietnam. It turns NASA FIRMS observations into interactive maps, calendars, and historical comparisons, making a complex satellite record easier to understand.

What it does

Users can select a region, a grid cell, or a rectangular area on the map and explore activity by year, month, five-day period, or day. They can compare different periods, examine seasonal patterns, and inspect the data sources behind the results. Vietnamese and English interfaces make the application accessible to both local and international audiences.

How it works

Our data combines MODIS observations from Terra and Aqua with VIIRS observations from Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21. These instruments have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities, so combining their raw counts can create misleading trends.

An offline Python pipeline cleans the observations, identifies persistent thermal sources, and aggregates activity into a 0.25° grid. It uses overlapping satellite records to calibrate detection counts onto a common Suomi-NPP-equivalent scale. The resulting dataset provides a more consistent basis for exploring historical activity.

The application also preserves information about where each value comes from: direct observations, cross-satellite scaling, or model estimates. Users can inspect this provenance alongside historical comparisons.

Benefits and intended impact

Hoa Lich helps students, researchers, journalists, and environmental organizations investigate when and where burning activity is concentrated. It supports questions such as: How does this month compare with the same month in previous years? When does activity usually peak? How do patterns differ between regions?

Our intended impact is to make Earth observation data more accessible and encourage informed investigation of environmental change. The application supports historical analysis rather than emergency response or fire prediction.

Tools and technologies

We used Python, pandas, and NumPy for data processing and analysis; Java 21 and Spring Boot for the backend API; and React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend. Git and GitHub supported collaboration and version control. Precomputed data artifacts allow the backend to serve queries without rerunning the harmonization pipeline for each request.

What makes the project creative

Hoa Lich connects cross-satellite harmonization with an interface designed around questions people can ask about their own region. Maps show spatial patterns, calendars reveal timing, and historical charts provide context. Data provenance is part of the user experience, helping people understand how a result was produced.

Factors we considered

We considered differences in sensor resolution, satellite coverage, observation times, missing data, persistent industrial heat sources, and the distinction between archive and near-real-time products. We also considered performance, bilingual accessibility, and clear scientific communication.

A satellite detection is not necessarily an independent fire incident. Suomi-NPP-equivalent activity is not burned area, and an absence of detections does not prove an absence of fire. By making these limits visible, Hoa Lich helps users interpret historical patterns responsibly.
